sources.cite: Progressive care nursing certification exam handbook (July 2026), test plan 4C Behavioral/Psychosocial (3%), including suicidal ideation

sources.cite: NIMH, Ask Suicide-Screening Questions (ASQ) Toolkit, information sheet: four questions and a fifth acuity question asked after any yes; a yes to it is an acute positive, 'imminent risk', that needs a STAT safety and full mental health evaluation, and the patient 'cannot leave until evaluated for safety'; a non-acute positive needs a brief suicide safety assessment; refusing to answer counts as positive
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in NIMH's PDF (summarizing fetch with short quotes). The four questions: a wish to be dead, feeling others would be better off, thoughts of suicide in the past week, any attempt ever. 'Clinical judgment can always override a negative screen.' Validated for youth and adult medical patients, including adult medical inpatients (Horowitz et al., Psychosomatics 2020); the toolkit has emergency department, inpatient and outpatient pathways (NIMH adult toolkit page, read the same day). The questions are paraphrased in the sim.

sources.cite: NIMH, Adult ASQ Toolkit: Brief Suicide Safety Assessment guides, nursing scripts and suicide risk screening pathways for the emergency department, the inpatient medical/surgical unit and outpatient primary care and specialty clinics
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch): an index page; the pathways themselves were not opened, so what each setting does after a positive screen is taken from the information sheet.

sources.cite: The Joint Commission, R3 Report Issue 18: National Patient Safety Goal for suicide prevention, NPSG.15.01.01 (effective 2019-07-01): EP1 environmental risk assessment; EP2 screen 'using a validated screening tool'; EP3 an assessment that 'directly asks about suicidal ideation, plan, intent, suicidal or self-harm behaviors'; EP4 document the risk level and the mitigation plan; EP5-EP7 policies for monitoring, discharge counseling and follow-up
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch with quotes; issue dated 2019-11-20, updated 2025-12-03). The report names one-to-one monitoring as a key protocol on nonpsychiatric units; it does not itself require it, so the observation level in each sim is the facility's policy.

sources.cite: The Columbia Lighthouse Project, Columbia Protocol (C-SSRS) triage page: 'the most worrisome answers are a recent (past month) yes to items 4 or 5' (intent, intent with a plan) 'and/or any recent (3 months) behavior'; next steps 'are setting specific', and 'interventions should be changed to reflect your individual resources and policies'
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 (summarizing fetch with quotes; page last modified 2024-03-22). The screener's items, relayed from the NCMHCE session (read 2026-11-11): wish to be dead; suicidal thoughts; thoughts with method; intent without plan; intent with plan; suicidal behavior.

sources.cite: SAMHSA, SAFE-T: Suicide Assessment Five-Step Evaluation and Triage (PEP24-01-036): identify risk and protective factors, conduct a suicide inquiry, determine the risk level and interventions, and document a treatment plan
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 on SAMHSA's product page (summarizing fetch). The page names the activities without the card's risk-level table, which was not read.

brief.situation: Ruth Callahan, 67 (a fictional patient), is on day 3 of a progressive care stay for newly diagnosed heart failure with a low ejection fraction. Her diuresis is going well and she is due home in two days. At 21:30, as you check her evening vital signs, she says quietly, 'My family would be better off without me. I'm just a burden now.' She lives with her husband, who has early dementia; her daughter lives an hour away. The hospital screens patients for suicide risk with a validated tool when there is a cue. You are her nurse, with three other patients; you have about 30 minutes before your next round.
handover: Day 3, new heart failure; diuresing well; telemetry sinus rhythm. Low mood noted by the day nurse; no mental health history in the chart.
Unit policy: any positive suicide screen gets a patient safety attendant (constant observation) and a room check until the provider's brief suicide safety assessment.
howItWorks: Choose what to ask and how to respond from the action groups. Ruth answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the clock by the minutes that exchange took.
Her trust, distress and how much she discloses change with what you say.
Your time ends at 30 minutes. Afterward you write a short risk formulation, then document the risk level and disposition.

source.note: About 30 minutes before the next round on a progressive care unit with four patients (author's scenario timing).
How trust and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a patient.

checkIn.label: Sit down: 'That sounded heavy. Tell me more.'

effects.log: You sit beside her and ask her to say more.

effects.finding: "Tom can't manage without me, and now I can't manage at all."

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what was said, without judging it.

effects.finding: She nods. "Yes. That's what it feels like."

effects.log: You ask the four screening questions directly.

then.finding: "Yes, I've wished I were dead. Yes, they'd be better off. And yes, this week I've thought about killing myself." No past attempt.

then.log: Positive screen: a wish to be dead, feeling a burden and suicidal thoughts this week; no past attempt.

then.finding: "Oh, I'm just tired, dear. Don't mind me." (Not yet enough trust to answer honestly.)

formulation.question: Write your risk formulation for Ruth: her risk level and why, and what you put in place.

parts.label: Risk level and reasons
parts.criteria: Names a non-acute positive screen: a wish to be dead, feeling a burden, suicidal thoughts this week, no thoughts right now, no plan or intent, no attempt; risk factors: new serious illness, low mood two weeks, poor sleep, caregiver strain; protective: her granddaughter, daughter, faith.
parts.modelAnswer: Non-acute positive: a wish to be dead, feeling a burden and suicidal thoughts at night this week, but none right now, no plan, no intent and no past attempt. New heart failure, two weeks of low mood and poor sleep, and caring for her husband add risk; her granddaughter, her daughter and her faith protect.

safe.headline: Good: safe through the night
safe.body: You heard the cue, screened early, followed up directly and put observation, a room check and the right people in place.

unsafe.headline: Left at foreseeable risk
unsafe.body: 'Better off without me' is the burden question of the screen itself. It calls for the screen, observation and a report the same night.

walkout.headline: The conversation broke
walkout.body: False cheer and advice tell a patient her feelings are not welcome here. Reflection and direct questions keep her talking.

scoring.modelReasoning: Feeling like a burden is one of the screening questions, so her words are a cue to screen at once, not to reassure. A positive screen with no thoughts right now is non-acute: she needs a brief suicide safety assessment before discharge, and on this unit, constant observation and a room check until then. The nurse calls the provider, writes the handoff and involves family with consent; a promise not to act is never a safety measure.
